facts.raw_span: A man in his 40s presented with a 10-year history of pruritic lesions on the scrotum and buttock
pruritic lesions on the scrotum and buttock
He was previously treated at a local clinic with little improvement
He had no relevant medical history and no family history of similar skin problems
Scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center and a slightly elevated edge on the scrotum, buttock, groin, and intergluteal cleft
There was no inguinal adenopathy
Routine blood work, including blood biochemistry, syphilis serologies, and HIV testing, were normal or negative

Revealed hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic columns (cornoid lamella) overlying dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and hypogranulosis with a perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis

hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic column (cornoid lamella), and several dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the epidermal invagination with hypogranulosis and perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center and a slightly elevated edge, along with histopathological findings of hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, and parakeratotic columns, is consistent with Darier disease.
The patient's symptoms and histopathological findings could also be consistent with Grover disease, which is characterized by transient acantholytic dermatosis.

The patient's presentation of well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques could also be consistent with psoriasis, although the lack of other characteristic features such as scaling and silvery plaques makes this diagnosis less likely.
The patient's symptoms and histopathological findings could also be consistent with lichen planus, which is characterized by an inflammatory condition affecting the skin and mucous membranes.

The patient's presentation of well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques could also be consistent with seborrheic keratosis, although the lack of other characteristic features such as a warty or verrucous appearance makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's histopathological findings of dyskeratotic keratinocytes and hyperkeratosis could be consistent with dyskeratosis congenita, although the lack of other characteristic features such as nail dystrophy and oral leukoplakia makes this diagnosis less likely.
It explains the biopsy findings showing hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic column, and dyskeratotic keratinocytes.
